# Results — Study 711 ("A Birkin beats the S&P and gold")

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Does an Hermès Birkin really
out-return stocks and gold, as the Baghunter/Credit-Suisse-cited "14.2%/yr, never a down
year" number claims? We test the strongest tradable version: a secondary-market **Birkin
resale index** (hardcoded, cited, **approximate** — a labelled proxy, not a live feed) and
the only **listed** ways to buy the trade (Hermès `RMS.PA`, LVMH `MC.PA`, Kering `KER.PA`),
each benchmarked against `SPY` and `GLD`. Offline & deterministic; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Birkin resale index | **Hardcoded, cited, approximate** annual secondary-market level (base 100 @ 2015-12-31), reconstructed from the Baghunter 2016 headline + Knight Frank Luxury Investment Index + press reporting — see [`docs/references.md`](references.md). **A PROXY, not a feed.** |
| Equity proxies | `RMS.PA` (Hermès) · `MC.PA` (LVMH) · `KER.PA` (Kering) — month-end Adj Close via yfinance, cached under `_cache/` |
| Benchmarks | `SPY` (S&P 500) and `GLD` (gold) — the two assets the claim names — month-end Adj Close, yfinance |
| As-of | 2025-12-31 (month-end; no partial-year bar) |
| Equity window | 2015-01 → 2025-12 (132 months; 131 monthly returns per name) |

> **Why a proxy, stated as a decision.** There is no free, live, API-available handbag
> resale index. Rather than fabricate a live tape we (a) hardcode a small, clearly-cited,
> **approximate** annual series whose *shape* — steady retail-driven appreciation, a
> 2020–22 melt-up, the 2023–24 luxury-handbag cooling — is the load-bearing public fact,
> and (b) test the **tradable** equity proxies a public investor can actually buy. A
> maison's equity is **not** the resale price of a Birkin; it is a labelled proxy throughout.

## The claim, quoted

Baghunter (2016) reported a Birkin returned **≈14.2%/yr over 1980–2015**, "never a down
year," beating the S&P (quoted at ≈8.7%) and gold. That is a cherry-picked, survivorship-
laden window; below we test the modern, measurable, net-of-cost reality.

## Half 1 — did the Birkin beat the S&P and gold? (resale index vs SPY & GLD)

The (approximate, cited) Birkin secondary-market index, year-end levels base 100:

| year | 2015 | 2016 | 2017 | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| level | 100 | 106 | 113 | 121 | 128 | 134 | 150 | 162 | **166** | 158 | 163 |
| YoY | — | +6.0% | +6.6% | +7.1% | +5.8% | +4.7% | +11.9% | +8.0% | +2.5% | **−4.8%** | +3.2% |

Headline risk/return vs the two benchmarks the claim names:

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **Birkin resale index** | **+5.01%** | 4.4% | **−4.8%** |
| SPY (year-end) | **+14.71%** | 15.7% | −18.2% |
| GLD (year-end) | **+14.60%** | 19.9% | −4.9% |

**The bag lost both races outright:** ~5%/yr vs ~15%/yr for the S&P and ~15%/yr for gold.
Its one virtue is *low volatility* — a genuine store-of-value trait — but on **return** it
trails. The mean annual excess (index − benchmark) is:

- **vs SPY: −10.71%/yr, t = −1.95** (p = 0.083, n = 10 years)
- **vs GLD: −10.88%/yr, t = −1.52** (p = 0.162, n = 10 years)

Neither excess clears |t| ≥ 2, but both point estimates are large *negatives*: the honest
read is "no evidence the Birkin beats stocks or gold, and it likely underperformed both."

## Half 2 — the tradable maisons vs SPY (the only thing you can buy)

Monthly Adj Close, Newey-West (6-lag) alpha vs SPY. **These are labelled proxies.**

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max DD | alpha/yr | beta | NW *t*(α) | p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **RMS.PA** (Hermès) | **+20.85%** | 24.5% | 0.90 | −35.0% | **+11.88%** | 0.76 | **+1.93** | 0.055 |
| **MC.PA** (LVMH) | +16.85% | 24.1% | 0.77 | −46.8% | +6.16% | 0.89 | +0.93 | 0.354 |
| **KER.PA** (Kering) | +7.97% | 31.3% | 0.40 | **−74.3%** | −1.64% | 1.00 | −0.18 | 0.855 |
| SPY | +13.84% | 15.0% | 0.95 | −23.9% | — | — | — | — |
| GLD | +11.28% | 14.3% | 0.82 | −18.1% | — | — | — | — |

The claim's **best card** is Hermès the *stock*: it out-returned SPY with a **+11.9%/yr**
alpha — but at Newey-West **t = 1.93**, just **under** the *t* ≥ 2 bar, so `REAL` is *not*
earned (it reads `WEAK` at most). LVMH is insignificant and Kering is *negative* with a
**−74%** drawdown. And decisively: this is the *equity of a diversified luxury company*
(watches, leather, beauty, fashion, buybacks), **not the resale price of a Birkin**.

## Half 3 — the consignment/illiquidity haircut (what a flip really costs)

The pitch never charges the friction. A buy-at-a-premium / sell-through-consignment round
trip costs ~**30%** (specialist reseller / auction consignment ~25–33% + the buy-side
grey-market premium), amortised over a ~**3-year** hold, plus ~**0.5%/yr** insurance/
storage/authentication. Charged once on the index's gross CAGR:

| | value |
|---|--:|
| gross CAGR (index) | +5.01%/yr |
| − consignment-spread drag (30% over 3y) | −11.21%/yr |
| − insurance/carry | −0.50%/yr |
| **= NET CAGR a real flipper earns** | **−7.23%/yr** |

The +5% gross *that already lost to both stocks and gold* turns **negative** once you pay
to actually transact and hold the physical bag. A savings account beat it.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic, fixed-seed "steady compounder" path (planted +12%/yr drift, σ = 3%/mo,
seed 711): the inference engine recovers the planted up-sign and a finite Sharpe — peak
≈ 316 → end ≈ 270, recovered CAGR **+10.54%**, Sharpe 1.00, max DD −21.8%, `sign_ok = 1`.
The harness can bank a planted signal, so a null on the real proxies is a real null, not a
broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE (it *under*-performs).** Over 2015–2025 the resale index returned ~5%/yr
  vs ~15%/yr for SPY and ~15%/yr for gold; the annual excess is **−10.7%/yr (t = −1.95)**
  vs SPY and **−10.9%/yr (t = −1.52)** vs gold — no evidence the bag beats either, and the
  point estimates are sharply negative. The single closest leg, RMS.PA equity, is NW
  **t = 1.93 < 2** — WEAK at most, and it isn't the handbag.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The gross index CAGR (5.0%) goes **negative (−7.2%/yr)** after a
  realistic ~30% consignment spread + carry; the buyable proxies are single-stock luxury
  beta (KER.PA −74%, β≈1). Illiquid, wide-spread, no scalable book.
- **"Beats stocks & gold?" — BUSTED.** On return and net-of-cost the bag loses to **both**
  assets the headline names. The famous 14.2%/yr is a cherry-picked 1980–2015 window with
  survivorship baked in — a marketing statistic, not a tradable asset class.

> **Caveat (named, not buried).** The Birkin index here is a **small, hardcoded,
> approximate** reconstruction of public reporting — its *level path/shape* is defensible
> but its precise year-end values are not a live feed, and the annual *t* rests on just 10
> observations. The equity proxies are exactly that — proxies for "owning the luxury-bag
> trade," not the resale price of a bag; and the index's own level survivorship (bags that
> stop trading drop out) biases the claim **upward**, not down. All limitations push the
> verdict toward humility, not toward a stronger claim: nothing here says a Birkin beats
> stocks or gold, and several lines say the opposite.
